Architecture

A developer's path through the whole system

Loopflow records commands, preserves agent conversations, and drives Graphs. Process records an lf command and its outcome; LfSession records a conversation; a Graph is one lf process and the step processes it starts. What runs on a Machine shows where chats, batches, work sessions and workers run and which processes keep them alive.

This guide specifies the accepted model. The reference owns cutover status, the remaining work map and the checked current-source inventory.

This guide is for developers changing Loopflow. It starts with the smallest complete path, then opens into the areas that own the system. Command syntax lives in the lf reference; the exhaustive checked inventory lives in Architecture Reference.

Run one Skill#

lf implement

That command discovers implement, assembles its context, chooses a provider, records its Process, reserves an LfSession, captures the input, then launches the provider. It needs no Wave, Task, or server process. The LfSession and its history survive the command, so a later command can reopen the conversation.

request
  |
  v
lf CLI --> Skill discovery --> prompt --> provider route --> harness
                                                          |
                                                          v
                                               LfSession history
                                               + immutable input/output artifacts

Before the provider starts, the current Machine has the conversation reservation and its immutable input. SQLite owns identity, attribution, attachment authority and history references; payload files retain large captured inputs and output. Admission failure stops before provider launch. General command logging has a different boundary: unavailable/bootstrap stores leave explicitly unrecorded Processes rather than bypassing installation authority to create a receipt.

LfSession history records provider outcomes, retries and usage. Process records the command's outcome. A provider can finish successfully before a later command operation fails; neither result overwrites the other. Missing telemetry stays missing. The execution contract defines these ownership boundaries.

The implementation follows the same order as the diagram:

Stage Concrete owner Produces
Parse and dispatch lf/mod.rs One command and launch context
Find the Skill skills/catalog.rs One selected Skill source
Assemble context prompt/mod.rs System and task prompts
Select the model and harness agent/mod.rs Configured launch and headless fallback order
Launch and normalize harness/ Provider output and usage events
Record command and conversation evidence journal/ and the store Process completion, LfSession history and immutable payloads

Follow the complete execution path →

Add one capability at a time#

The Skill runner is useful by itself. The rest of Loopflow grows outward by adding one kind of capability at each layer. Tracked Work owns autonomous progression; attributed conversations consume the same execution and delivery operations available to helpers without becoming standing Work identities.

one Skill run
    |
    +-- Graph: compose Skills, mechanical operations, and review boundaries
    |
    +-- Work: preserve purpose and input across independent processes
    |
    +-- Task delivery: bind concrete Work to one active remote branch, worktree, and PR
    |
    +-- Controllers: pursue Work end to end using the layers above
    |
    +-- Machine: place execution, credentials, services, files, and locks
    |
    `-- Views: project planning, command, conversation, provider, Git, and OS evidence
Area What it adds Start here
Execution Skill discovery, prompt assembly, provider routing, harnesses, command and conversation history Execution
Planning Graph composition, Wave/Task Work, Steer, questions, review GraphSteps Planning
Delivery Managed worktrees, commits, one active Task branch/PR, CI repair, merge Delivery
Machines Execution destinations, Task ownership and SSH routing Machines and processes
Terminals Where an agent runs, held terminals, views, headless work Transport
Client access and installation Server admission, registration/update and continuity across replacement Client API server
Data Truth owners, SQLite, files, external systems, projections, consistency Data and persistence
Codebase Source territories, public surfaces, processes, extension points Codebase map

The source tree makes the planning boundary literal:

work/
wave/{mod,config,context,
      memory,relocate}
project
task

ops/task.rs                   Task launch: a fresh Graph in the Task checkout
lf/commands/graph.rs           Graph process: one process per Graph

execution kernel: graph/ + agent/ + prompt/ + harness/ + command and conversation history
composition surfaces: lf/ + bin/

work never imports the Graph runner. The execution kernel works without either layer and never loads Work. CLI callers resolve Work identity and Wave memory, then pass ordinary launch inputs into the kernel.

Release delivery also separates proof from authority:

merged release commit
        |
        v
candidate ref --> hosted matrix --> signed artifact receipt
                                           |
                                           v
                                  immutable version tag
                                           |
                                           v
                                      publication

The candidate ref and receipt are disposable recovery state. The version tag is created only after the exact commit and artifact hashes are proven; retries after that point publish the same bytes under the same tag.

Each area page starts with a real command or artifact, follows its request or data flow, and ends with the contracts that neighboring areas may rely on.

What runs on a Machine#

lf implement                 # the agent is this command's child
lf resume --task LOO-12      # a view of a terminal the holder keeps
lf task run LOO-12           # starts a Graph process and returns
ps -axo command | grep '^lf '
# lf server run
# lf holder run
# lf --task task_… graph run

Three processes stay up: one Machine server, a holder for each build that still has agents, and a Graph process for each running Graph. Every other lf is a command that ends.

your terminal            lf <skill> ──────────────────────────► agent        chat
script or pipe           lf -b <skill> ───────────────────────► agent        batch

your terminal ─ view ─┐
Desktop pane  ─ view ─┼─► Machine server ─► holder ─► PTY ─► agent or shell   work session or Desktop shell
phone         ─ view ─┘         │
                                └─ store, hooks, steers, Work reads and writes

lf task run / lf task auto on ──────────► Graph process ─► step lf ─► agent          worker
        │                                │
        └─ one startup line, then gone   └─ logs/graph-<id>.log

Transport selects one of the four launch kinds before delegation. Managed launches report turns to the Machine server and require it at startup.

Launch Reports turns Where the agent runs Examples
Chat No In the caller's terminal, which owns its lifetime lf <skill> at a terminal, including lf research --task LOO-12
Batch No Headless under the caller, returning output to it lf -b <skill>
Work session Yes On a PTY in a holder, independent of its viewers Task, Wave and repository conversations, or a conversation opened in a held terminal through Desktop or a framed lf --machine view
Worker Yes Headless, with its lifetime set by the step or caller Headless steps of lf task run or lf task auto on or landing's ci-fix

The checkout, --task and LF_AS supply Task attribution. Usage counts toward that Task, and hooks on every launch read the Session's steers from the store, including steers for that Task. Chats and batches use the launch's context; work sessions and workers also report boundaries so the server can refresh it.

Desktop Task shells use held terminals too. lf session list shows detached when a running conversation has no view.

Process One per Holds Restarts
Machine server (lf server run) Machine Client connections, hook boundaries, the registry of held terminals with one terminal emulator each, views, exit settlement On every install; the OS supervisor keeps it up
Holder (lf holder run) Build with live terminals PTYs, their children, a ring of recent output per PTY. No store, no Sessions Never; it exits when its last terminal ends
Graph process (lf … graph run) Running Graph The graph, its cursor and its step children Never; a stopped Graph is history and lf task run starts a fresh one

What survives what follows from that table. Closing a view ends nothing. Restarting or upgrading the server ends nothing: it greets the holders it finds, rebuilds each screen from the holder's ring and carries on, and views reconnect at the PTY byte they had reached. An install replaces the server and leaves holders on the build that started them, so a conversation keeps its build until it is quit and resumed. Killing the lf task run that started a Graph leaves the Graph running. Logout and reboot end every process; Sessions and Graph history remain, and lf resume or lf task run starts new ones.

The server is in no agent's byte path except as the relay between a held PTY and its views. A hook that cannot reach it logs a gap and the turn continues; a holder that loses it keeps its agents and says nothing about them. The store is opened by whichever process is writing: commands, Graph processes and the server. The holder never opens it.

Conversations started by a build from before held terminals run under an lf session serve process of their own until their agent quits. Nothing starts one now, and nothing sweeps them. lf resume of one, or opening its Desktop pane, restarts it: lf ends that process by its verified pid and birth, waits for it to exit and resumes the thread from provider history where any resume of it would run: in a held terminal for a work session, in the caller's terminal for a chat. One it cannot verify, or that does not exit, keeps running and the message names its pid.

The transport README owns the holder and view protocols; the server README owns client operations and hook boundaries.

The whole system#

                                      shared truth
                              planning   GitHub     providers
                                 ^          ^           ^
                                 |          |           |
user / agent --> lf CLI --------+----------+-----------+
                    |
          +---------+----------+
          |                    |
          v                    v
  authored definitions    tracked Work
  Skills / Graphs /       Wave -> Task
  goals / memory                  |
          |                       +---------> Task delivery
          |                       |                ^
          |                       v                |
          +------------> Task advancement --------+
          |                       |
          +-----------------------+ Skill boundary
                                  v
                       shared execution components
              discovery / prompt / route / harness
                              |
                              v
                        Process / LfSession
                              |
                              v
                  status / planning / usage / app

another machine is another Machine; cross it explicitly with `lf --machine`

Each Machine's server also admits clients: Desktop over a private socket, and a paired phone over an authenticated connection (client API server). It does not centralize execution across Machines. Machine routing selects where commands run, the server admits clients, and installation owns server registration and updates. A Machine owns its processes, credentials, planning store, execution history, and OS locks. Repository files carry authored definitions and memory. The tracker (Git, Linear or Asana) and GitHub keep shared planning and delivery truth. Readers join those sources; they do not replace them with a universal ledger.

Core models#

Repository
  |-- Task                    repository work, optionally outside a Wave
  `-- Wave                    enduring objective, memory, cadence and default graph
        `-- Project           a group of Tasks that starts and ends; optional provider binding
              `-- Task        identity, worktree, PR and captured graph position

Process                          one actual lf process; immutable causal parent
LfSession                  one conversation; nullable attached LfProcess
  `-- history                 provider starts, outcomes, retries and usage
Graph                          one lf process; cursor in its memory, graph in GraphProcess
  `-- step processes              plain commands; the Graph process records each one's node
Model Represents Primary truth
Skill Reusable instructions and declared context Repository, builtin or installed Markdown
Graph Reusable graph of agent, mechanical and routing steps Repository or builtin YAML
Process One actual lf process, its caller and command completion processes
LfSession An interactive or headless conversation across attachments and native reconnection agent_sessions, subordinate history and provider-native conversation
Running Graph One Graph process and the steps it starts, including taskless execution The Graph process and its child step processes in processes
Wave Enduring objective, memory, cadence and budget Wave files, local Wave identity and its one Project, linked to a Linear Project when connected
Project All of a Wave’s Tasks, grouped under one name, summary and status projects row, shared through the tracker
Task A concrete change, investigation or document tasks, the tracker, Git and GitHub
Steer An authored correction to Work Ordered Work input
Machine A machine's store, credentials and exact process authority Machine identity and observed route
Task ownership Who works on a Task, on which Machine, or unowned Append-only task_ownership log; each person's Machine-local Wave → Machine default places their unowned Work

An LfSession keeps its ID, name, feedback and native conversation when its command process changes. Its interactive field is independent of purpose, Graph membership and completion. Default conversation views show interactive Sessions; explicit filters expose headless and completed history. Large captured payloads remain files, but readers select and page rows before opening them.

Connect uses the live AgentProcess when possible. Passive display acquires no claim. Transferring the attachment revokes the old client's ability to start or steer turns and mutate Session state, including queued writes. It does not replace the AgentProcess or interrupt an existing turn. Client replacement leaves the AgentProcess alive and never authorizes killing a shared one for one thread. AgentProcess PID, client PID and attached LfProcess are distinct.

Process ancestry records the actual lf caller. A direct child names its parent's Process; an agent-issued child also records via_agent and LfSession provenance. The provider's AgentProcess resolves to its attached LfProcess at child admission. A delayed command from a replaced provider retains historical provenance; old Process parents are never rewritten. Causal ancestry grants no control authority.

Every Graph started for a Task, by naming it or in its checkout, is part of its work. Only lf task run and lf task auto on advance the Task's captured graph position; independent Graphs leave that position unchanged. Each launch starts a fresh Graph process. Taskless and Task-owned Graphs use the same Graph runner. The Graph process holds the compiled graph and cursor in memory; template composition compiles into the graph, and loop passes are positions in it. Each step is a real child Process whose argv carries the Graph name, launch sequence and position. A step's result is how its process exited; a deciding or routing step also answers through the Session turn its Process captured. Mechanical work creates no agent conversation. A Session reaches its Graph through the step Process that captured its input. A killed Graph process leaves its Processes as history; nothing resumes it, and its caller launches fresh work.

Task requires repository identity and may belong to a Wave through its planning row. Constructors fill omitted ancestors and reject mismatches. Bind fills an unassigned conversation's Task once. CLI states the permanent target and writes; Desktop confirms it. Bind cannot clear or move an assignment or change Graph membership. Done and landed Tasks remain valid targets. Earlier usage retains its recorded owner; binding affects subsequent work, and uncertain mid-turn allocation remains unknown.

Reserving actual Task work (lf task run or lf task checkout allocating a checkout) claims an unowned Task in its append-only ownership log. Recording an inspection command's Process does not claim a Task. Missing history alone cannot prove untouched backlog; unrelated competing plans remain unresolved.

The reference owns the field and write contracts and the current-state conversion boundary. Process and LfSession are the execution owners; Run has no separate lifecycle.

Follow the common paths#

Direct work#

lf debug -c
lf qa --diff files

These commands need the execution area only: discover, prompt, route, launch, record, return.

Direct Task work#

lf checkout INF-123
lf --task INF-123 research "write scratch/runtime.md"
lf --task INF-123 research "write scratch/prompts.md"
lf commit -m "Reconcile Task research"
lf pr publish
lf pr submit
lf task status INF-123 --json

checkout creates or reuses tracked Task Work and its checkout placement without starting execution. Publication creates its optional, sole PR. Each --task command starts an independent LfSession in that worktree; several may overlap and write distinct scratch paths. Any caller may then use the ordinary Work and delivery commands. Those commands act on delivery facts, not on Graph-driving authority. submit and land therefore work the same whether the Task was pursued by a Task Graph, piecemeal helper LfSessions, or another system.

Task Graphs#

lf --wave product wave-operate        # one finite pass over your started Tasks
lf task run INF-123
lf --wave <wave> wave-operate "ship invoices first"
lf wave status product

task run places the Task and starts a fresh Graph process from its saved position, returning once the process registers. At the next breakpoint the Task conversation presents the finished work. Continuing takes the worker’s recommendation or carries a reply to the next worker. -b waits and takes the recommended path. lf task auto on approves continuation through delivery. A stopped process stays history. A direct lf --task ISSUE graph GRAPH uses the same runner without moving the Task's graph position. Replanning keeps existing Task identity and execution. See Task workflows.

Another machine#

lf --machine build-home session list --json
lf --machine build-home --wave product wave-operate

The origin transports one command. The target resolves its own Machine state and runs the same lf. Reads are local unless this hop is explicit.

How to read the code#

Start with the area that owns the behavior, then follow the object passed to the next area. Do not begin with the storage implementation unless storage is the behavior.

If you are changing… Read
provider launch, retries, usage, or telemetry Execution
Graph semantics, Work state, Steer, questions, review GraphSteps and Task advancement Planning
worktrees, commits, PR ranges, checks, or landing Delivery
remote execution, Task ownership, process control, promotion Machines and processes
where an agent runs, held terminals, views, headless launches Transport
client operations, hook boundaries, subscriptions Server
schema, files, projections, DTOs, or consistency Data and persistence
module ownership, APIs, binaries, routes, or code size Codebase map

For exhaustive lookup, open the checked architecture reference. Its bounded checker compares CLI families, process boundaries, SQLite tables, HTTP routes, providers, subprocess edges, projections, and historical vocabulary. A successful check covers that inventory, not configured runtime behavior.

Research#

Session experience comparison reviews T3 Code, Paradev and Paseo commit history and tests, with Loopflow findings and Task handoffs. It records source observations from November 2026, not a live product benchmark.
